content: The guidelines recommend dual therapy for gonorrhea due to increasing antimicrobial resistance. For Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the preferred treatment is a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg combined with a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g. Alternatively, a single oral dose of cefixime 400 mg can be used with azithromycin 1 g. If local antimicrobial resistance data confirm susceptibility, monotherapy with ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly or cefixime 400 mg orally may be considered. For Chlamydia trachomatis, the treatment includes doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. If azithromycin was not included in gonorrhea therapy, a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 7 days can be used. Alternatively, ofloxacin 200–400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days is an option. For Mycoplasma genitalium, azithromycin is recommended at 500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg daily for days 2–5, provided there is no macrolide resistance. The World Health Organization (WHO) is revising treatment recommendations for gonorrhea and M. genitalium due to rising resistance to azithromycin and reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is caused by pathogens such as N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis, as well as facultative gram-negative rods and mycoplasmas. Differentiating between these pathogens clinically is challenging, so treatment regimens must cover a broad range of organisms. For sexually active women presenting with lower abdominal pain and clinical signs such as cervical motion tenderness or lower abdominal tenderness, treatment for PID should be initiated immediately. Testing for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and M. genitalium is recommended to support partner management. Hospitalization for acute PID should be considered in cases of diagnostic uncertainty, suspected surgical emergencies (e.g., appendicitis or ectopic pregnancy), pelvic abscess, severe illness, pregnancy, inability to tolerate outpatient therapy, or failure to respond to outpatient treatment. For genital ulcer disease, the most common causes globally are herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2). Other causes include Treponema pallidum (syphilis), C. trachomatis serovars L1–L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum), and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid). Clinical differentiation of genital ulcers is often inaccurate, so management should rely on laboratory-based etiological studies or a syndromic approach guided by local epidemiological data. Primary syphilis presents as a painless ulcer (chancre) at the site of infection, typically appearing three weeks after exposure. If untreated, the ulcer heals spontaneously, but the infection progresses to secondary syphilis, characterized by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and rash. Secondary syphilis can lead to latency and, eventually, tertiary syphilis if untreated. For genital herpes, first-episode infections often present with systemic symptoms (fever, headache, malaise) and localized symptoms (pain, itching, dysuria, and vesicular or ulcerative lesions). Recurrent episodes are typically milder and shorter in duration. Diagnosis can be confirmed through PCR testing of lesion swabs, which is the most sensitive and specific method. Culture methods and serology may also be used but have limitations. In summary, the management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) requires a combination of clinical judgment, laboratory testing, and syndromic approaches to ensure effective treatment and minimize complications such as chronic pelvic pain, infertility, and transmission to partners.
